# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/main/src/RecoverySpell.sol#L165-L317


# Vulnerability details

## Description

When recovery spells are created, users preset the new owners of the safe that will be swapped. This is set at the wallet creation time, as the owners used will be part of the creation salt that is used to compute the recovery spell address. Recovery spells don't allow users to remove or add owners to that list.

In case 1 of the "new owners" is compromised and the recovery spell is used, that compromised owner will be injected as an owner in the safe's owners list, knowing that the previous owners are aware of this compromisation but had no solution to solve it.

This leads to the full compromisation of a wallet.

## Proof of Concept
1. User A predicts the safe address using `AddressCalculation::calculateAddress`.
2. User A uses the safe's predicted address to predict a recovery spell whose owners are users C and D.
3. User A creates the safe while passing the owners as users A and B and passing the recovery spell predicted address in step 2 as the recovery spell.
4. User A deploys the recovery spell.
**At this point we assume both users B and D are compromised**
5. User A initiates the wallet recovery by calling `executeRecovery` on the created spell, however, the issue here is that the new owners that will be replaced contain a compromised owner which is D.
6. At this point, user C can't directly remove D from the owners list in the save, as it'll require a time-locked transaction through the timelock, which is the same time user D will have to wait to execute a malicious transaction.

This results in a messed-up wallet, where a compromised owner is forcefully injected into the safe. As users before knew it was compromised but couldn't remove it.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Allow users to add/remove recovery spell owners, which can be done by other owners signing that transaction.



## Assessed type

Error

# Vulnerability details

## Summary
The Kleidi protocol's contracts are built using Solidity version 0.8.25, which includes the BLOBBASEFEE opcode (introduced in Solidity v0.8.24). However, this opcode is currently not supported on the Arbitrum network, as shown in this [screenshot](https://ibb.co/41nZV0N). This lack of support prevents the deployment of Kleidi contracts on Arbitrum, which is the intended network for deployment as stated in the contest page's [Scoping Q&A section](https://code4rena.com/audits/2024-10-kleidi): "Chains the protocol will be deployed on: Arbitrum, Ethereum, Optimism, Base."

## Proof of Concept
The Kleidi project's smart contracts use Solidity version 0.8.25, which incorporates the BLOBBASEFEE opcode, introduced in Solidity v0.8.24 as noted [here](https://github.com/ethereum/solidity/releases/tag/v0.8.24). However, as of the time of this report, the Arbitrum chain does not support this opcode, making deployment with this Solidity version impossible. According to the C4 documentation, this would correspond to a severity level of "2 — Med: Assets not at direct risk, but the function of the protocol or its availability could be impacted." The inability to deploy on Arbitrum exactly impacts the protocol's availability and functionality on the network, so this issue is marked as Medium severity.

## Impact
The project cannot currently be deployed on the Arbitrum network.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider using a different version of Solidity for the Arbitrum network. Alternatively, if you prefer deploying with Solidity v0.8.25, you can use this [tool](https://www.evmdiff.com/features?feature=opcodes) to check if Arbitrum has added support for the BLOBBASEFEE opcode.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/RecoverySpell.sol#L51
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/RecoverySpell.sol#L56


# Vulnerability details

## Summary
The `RecoverySpell` contract is a critical component of the Kleidi system, intended to enable secure recovery of Safe accounts in the event that an owner loses access to their private key. However, the contract’s design makes the recovery threshold immutable, meaning it cannot be adjusted once set. This inflexibility poses a risk: if one of the recovery participants also loses their access key, it becomes impossible to meet the threshold required for recovery. This design flaw undermines one of the primary functions of the Kleidi system, potentially locking users out of their funds.

## Proof of Concept
In `RecoverySpell`, the [`threshold`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/RecoverySpell.sol#L51) and [`recoveryThreshold`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/RecoverySpell.sol#L56) values are defined as immutable, meaning they are assigned at deployment and cannot be modified later. If an owner (Joe) creates a `RecoverySpell` module with a threshold based on his wife, son, and friend as authorized participants, but later, one of these participants also loses their key, recovery becomes impossible due to the fixed threshold. This inability to adapt in emergencies prevents Joe from recovering his Safe, ultimately blocking access to his funds forever.

## Impact
The inability to adjust recovery thresholds results in a critical loss of flexibility in emergency scenarios. If a recovery participant loses their key, the immutability of the threshold blocks the entire recovery process. This can effectively render the Safe unrecoverable, exposing users to potential loss of funds, particularly in multi-participant recovery setups.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Introduce a mechanism to adjust the recovery threshold dynamically if needed in emergency cases. One approach would be to allow a majority of participants (e.g., `recoveryAddressArr.length - 1`) to approve a reset of the threshold under special conditions. This would maintain security while providing critical flexibility for recovery in cases where one or more participants are unavailable.

# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept
totalOperations count can change by more than 1 in a single function call. The `_execute()` function allows arbitrary external calls without restricting changes to totalOperations. The `_execute` function performs an unchecked external call to an arbitrary target contract. This call can execute any code, including operations that modify the Timelock contract's state multiple times. totalOperations count, which is expected to change by at most 1 per function call, can be manipulated to change by more than 1.

For example, consider this sequence of events

1. A user calls the `execute` function on the Timelock contract.
2. The `execute` function internally calls `_execute`.
3. `_execute` makes an external call to a malicious contract.
4. The malicious contract performs multiple operations that each increment
5. The `_execute` function completes, but total Operation has changed by more than 1.

In [Timelock.sol:1021-1026](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L1021-L1026), the vulnerable code path
```solidity
function _execute(address target, uint256 value, bytes calldata data)
    private
{
    (bool success,) = target.call{value: value}(data); // <@Audit Vulnerable external call
    require(success, "Timelock: underlying transaction reverted");
}
```
The vulnerability lies in the unchecked external call that allows arbitrary execution. This can lead to unexpected state changes.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
1. Implement a wrapper or proxy pattern to control external interactions

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/c474b9480850d08514c100b415efcbc962608c62/src/RecoverySpellFactory.sol#L44-L78

# Vulnerability details

## Explanation
In case different chains are using the same recovery spell, certain attack vectors are possible:
(1) In case one of the chains has undergone a recovery that other chains haven't, and the new owners are compromised, the wallets on other chains can be enforced to change to the compromised keys. 
(2) Once the recovery spell on one of the chains has been created, those can be created on other chains as well and start the timer on `recoveryInitiated + delay`

## Impact
The precondition on this issue is that wallets on different chains use the same set of revcovery spells.
Since the protocol can not enforce the different recovery spells, once the first set of keys on all chains is compromised, if different networks on different chains do not migrate via the same module they all can be attacked.

## Proof of Concept
- Two wallets on Ethereum and Optimism have two recovery spells `A`, and `B`
- Original owners get compromised so Ethereum changes to `A`, and Optimism changes to `B`
- If the Ethereum's new keys get compromised as well, the attackers can create the recovery spell on Optimism and enforce the wallet on optimism to change to the compromised owners as well. This can happen after attackers use the stolen keys to create valid signatures to call `executeRecovery` with.
- Attackers need to take control of one of the new chains to take over all others.


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Ensure users use different recovery spells on different networks.

# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept
The [`revokeHotSigner`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L799-L804) function is designed to revoke the hot signer role from a specific address. The comment associated with this function states that it can be called by either the Safe or the Timelock. However, in the actual implementation, the `onlySafe` modifier is used, which restricts access to only the Safe, excluding the Timelock from calling the function.
```solidity
    /// @notice function to revoke the hot signer role from an address
>   /// can only be called by the timelock or the safe
    /// @param deprecatedHotSigner the address of the hot signer to revoke
>   function revokeHotSigner(address deprecatedHotSigner) external onlySafe { 
        _revokeRole(HOT_SIGNER_ROLE, deprecatedHotSigner);
    }
```
The comment suggests that both the Safe and the Timelock are allowed to call this function. The `onlySafe` modifier restricts access, so only the Safe can call it. If the Timelock contract attempts to call the function, the transaction will revert due to the `onlySafe` restriction.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Update the implementation to allow both the Safe and the Timelock to call the `revokeHotSigner` function by introducing a new modifier or extending the existing one to include both addresses.

```

The purpose of the salt is to ensure that the deployed contract addresses are unique, especially when using the `CREATE2` opcode, which allows for deterministic contract addresses based on the salt, the bytecode, and the deployer's address.
However, hardcoding the salt value poses a risk of address collisions if the contract is deployed multiple times with the same parameters. If two instances of the contract are deployed with the same salt and bytecode, they will result in the same address, leading to potential conflicts and unintended behavior.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Instead of using a hardcoded salt value, consider generating a unique salt for each deployment. This can be achieved by using a combination of the current block timestamp, the deployer's address, and a nonce.

The RecoverySpell contract contains contradictory comments regarding the configuration of the recovery delay relative to the timelock delay. This inconsistency can lead to security vulnerabilities or unintended behavior.
Edge Case description suggests that the recovery spell's delay should be longer than the timelock delay to allow current safe owners the opportunity to veto changes.
```solidity
If the time delay on a recovery spell is shorter than the timelock, the recovery spell can kick the safe owners without the current safe owners being able to veto this change. This is why it is important to have a longer time delay on the recovery spells than on the timelock.
```
Code Comment: States that the recovery spell's delay should be shorter than the timelock delay to ensure recovery actions can be executed before the timelock expires.

    /// @notice it is of critical importance that the delay is shorter
    /// than the timelock delay so that a recovery action can be executed
    /// before the timelock delay expires if need be. There is no way to enforce
    /// this in the contract, so it is up to the deployer to ensure that the
    /// delay is shorter than the timelock delay
```
**Impact**

**Shorter Delay:** May allow unauthorized recovery actions to bypass owner vetoes, posing a security risk.
**Longer Delay:** Could delay necessary recovery actions, potentially leaving the safe in a vulnerable state longer than intended.
**Example:** If a recovery spell is deployed with a delay shorter than the timelock, an attacker could potentially execute a recovery action before the current owners can respond, assuming they have the necessary signatures.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Update all comments and documentation to consistently reflect the intended configuration. This includes both inline comments and any external documentation provided to users. 
Clearly define the intended security model for the recovery delay in relation to the timelock. Decide whether the priority is quick recovery or owner oversight.

# Vulnerability details

## Summary

An insecure signature generation mechanism in the `InstanceDeployer.sol` contract allows for the creation of malformed ECDSA signatures. This flaw can potentially enable unauthorized transaction executions within the Gnosis Safe multisignature wallet, compromising the security and integrity of user assets managed by the Kleidi Wallet system.

## Vulnerability Details

### **1. Insecure Signature Construction**

The `InstanceDeployer.sol` contract constructs ECDSA signatures incorrectly by using predictable and non-standard components. This improper construction can lead to signature validation failures or unintended acceptance of invalid signatures.

```solidity
bytes32 r = bytes32(uint256(uint160(address(this))));
uint8 v = 1;
```

**Explanation:**  
Here, the `r` component of the ECDSA signature is derived directly from the contract's address, making it predictable. Additionally, the `v` value is hardcoded as `1`, whereas standard Ethereum signatures require `v` to be either `27` or `28`. This deviation from the standard signature format compromises the validity and security of the signature.

### **2. Incomplete Signature Components**

The signature constructed lacks the necessary `s` component, rendering it incomplete and potentially invalid.

```solidity
assembly ("memory-safe") {
    let ptr := mload(0x40)
    mstore(0x40, add(ptr, 97))
    mstore(ptr, 65)
    mstore(add(ptr, 0x20), r)
    mstore8(add(ptr, 0x60), v)
    signature := ptr
}
```

**Explanation:**  
In Ethereum's ECDSA signatures, the `s` component is crucial for ensuring the uniqueness and security of the signature. By omitting the `s` value, the signature fails to meet the necessary standards for validation, potentially allowing malformed signatures to bypass security checks.

### **3. Execution of Malformed Signature**

The malformed signature is used in the `execTransaction` method of the Gnosis Safe, which expects a valid ECDSA signature from authorized owners.

```solidity
require(
    Safe(payable(walletInstance.safe)).execTransaction(
        multicall3,
        0,
        abi.encodeWithSelector(IMulticall3.aggregate3.selector, calls3),
        Enum.Operation.DelegateCall,
        0,
        0,
        0,
        address(0),
        payable(0),
        signature
    ),
    "InstanceDeployer: Safe delegate call failed"
);
```

**Explanation:**  
The `execTransaction` function relies on valid signatures to authorize transactions. The use of an incomplete and non-standard signature (`r` derived from the contract's address and `v` set to `1`) can cause the transaction to either revert due to failed validation or, in the worst-case scenario, be incorrectly accepted, leading to unauthorized actions.

### **4. Potential for Unauthorized Transaction Execution**

If the Gnosis Safe's signature validation is bypassed due to the malformed signature, it can allow unauthorized entities to execute arbitrary transactions.

```solidity
bool success = safe.execTransaction(
    address(multicall3),
    0,
    abi.encodeWithSelector(IMulticall3.aggregate3.selector, calls3),
    Enum.Operation.DelegateCall,
    0,
    0,
    0,
    address(0),
    payable(0),
    signature
);
```

**Explanation:**  
The crafted signature might allow the `InstanceDeployer` to execute transactions on behalf of the Safe without proper owner approvals. This can lead to unauthorized changes in wallet configurations or unauthorized fund transfers, severely compromising the wallet's security.

## Impact

The insecure signature generation in `InstanceDeployer.sol` poses a significant risk to the Kleidi Wallet system:

- **Unauthorized Access:** Malformed signatures can potentially allow attackers to execute arbitrary transactions, leading to unauthorized access and control over the wallet.
  
- **Asset Loss:** Unauthorized transactions can result in the loss or theft of user assets managed by the multisig wallet.
  
- **Compromised Wallet Integrity:** The fundamental security model of the Kleidi Wallet relies on robust signature mechanisms. Weakening this mechanism undermines the entire system's integrity, making it vulnerable to various attacks.

## Tools Used

- **Foundry** 

## Recommendations

To remediate the identified vulnerability and enhance the security of the Kleidi Wallet system, the following measures are recommended:

### **1. Correct ECDSA Signature Generation**

- **Include All Signature Components:** Ensure that signatures include `r`, `s`, and `v` components. Utilize standard `v` values (`27` or `28`) as per Ethereum's specifications.
  
- **Use Trusted Libraries:** Leverage well-audited libraries like OpenZeppelin's `ECDSA` for signature generation and verification to prevent implementation flaws.

```solidity
bytes32 messageHash = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(/* message components */));
(bytes32 r, bytes32 s, uint8 v) = /* Generate signature using OpenZeppelin's ECDSA */;
bytes memory signature = abi.encodePacked(r, s, v);
```

**Explanation:**  
Using established libraries ensures that signatures are generated correctly, adhering to Ethereum's standards and enhancing security.

### **2. Enhance Signature Verification Logic**

- **Strict Validation:** Implement rigorous checks to verify the authenticity and integrity of signatures. Ensure that only valid and authorized signatures are accepted.
  
- **Enforce Multisig Thresholds:** Properly enforce the multisig threshold to require a minimum number of valid signatures for transaction approval, preventing single-point failures.

```solidity
require(
    ECDSA.recover(messageHash, signature) == authorizedOwner,
    "Invalid signature"
);
```

**Explanation:**  
Ensuring that signatures are both valid and from authorized owners prevents unauthorized transaction executions.

## Summary

A critical vulnerability has been identified in the `RecoverySpell.sol` contract of the Kleidi Wallet project. The issue arises from the improper use of assembly opcodes (`tload` and `tstore`) within the `executeRecovery` function, leading to flawed signature verification. This flaw either prevents the recovery mechanism from functioning or potentially allows unauthorized recovery operations, undermining the wallet's security.

## Vulnerability Details

### **Incorrect Assembly Opcode Usage**

The `executeRecovery` function employs non-existent EVM opcodes `tload` and `tstore` instead of the standard `sload` and `sstore` for storage operations. This misuse disrupts the intended signature verification process.

```solidity
assembly ("memory-safe") {
    valid := tload(recoveredAddress)
    if eq(valid, 1) { tstore(recoveredAddress, 0) }
}
```

**Explanation:**
- **Issue:** `tload` and `tstore` are **invalid EVM opcodes**. The correct opcodes for storage operations are `sload` (to read from storage) and `sstore` (to write to storage).
- **Consequence:** This results in **compilation errors**, preventing the contract from deploying successfully. If hypothetically bypassed, it would cause the function to **revert at runtime**, rendering the `executeRecovery` function inoperative.

### **Flawed Signature Verification Logic**

Even if the assembly were corrected to use valid opcodes, the improper handling of storage slots can compromise signature verification integrity.

```solidity
bytes32 digest = getDigest();
for (uint256 i = 0; i < v.length; i++) {
    address recoveredAddress = ECDSA.recover(digest, v[i], r[i], s[i]);
    bool valid;

    assembly ("memory-safe") {
        valid := sload(recoveredAddressSlot)
        if eq(valid, 1) { sstore(recoveredAddressSlot, 0) }
    }

    require(
        valid && recoveredAddress != address(0),
        "RecoverySpell: Invalid signature"
    );
}
```

**Explanation:**
- **Issue:** Even with valid opcodes, mapping `recoveredAddress` directly to storage slots without proper slot calculation can lead to **incorrect verification**, potentially allowing unauthorized signatures to pass or valid signatures to fail.
- **Consequence:** This can either **block legitimate recovery operations** or **enable unauthorized access**, depending on the implementation flaws.

## Impact

- **Denial of Service (DoS):** Legitimate users are **unable to perform recovery operations**, potentially losing access to their assets.
- **Unauthorized Access:** If signature verification is bypassed, malicious actors could **execute recovery operations**, gaining unauthorized control over user wallets.
- **Trust Erosion:** Users may lose trust in the security of the Kleidi Wallet, impacting the project's reputation and user base.

## Tools Used

- **Manual Code Review** 

## Recommendations

### **1. Correct Assembly Opcode Usage**

- **Replace Invalid Opcodes:**
  
  ```solidity
  assembly ("memory-safe") {
      valid := sload(recoveredAddressSlot)
      if eq(valid, 1) { sstore(recoveredAddressSlot, 0) }
  }
  ```

  - **Action:** Use `sload` and `sstore` instead of `tload` and `tstore`.
  - **Note:** Ensure that `recoveredAddressSlot` correctly maps to the intended storage slot.

### **2. Utilize Established Libraries for Signature Verification**

- **Leverage OpenZeppelin's ECDSA Library:**
  
  ```solidity
  require(
      ECDSA.recover(digest, v[i], r[i], s[i]) == owners[i],
      "RecoverySpell: Invalid signature"
  );
  ```

  - **Action:** Replace manual signature verification with trusted library functions to ensure security and correctness.

## Summary

A critical vulnerability has been identified in the `RecoverySpell.sol` contract of the Kleidi Wallet project. The contract utilizes non-standard EVM opcodes `tstore` and `tload` within assembly blocks. These opcodes are not recognized by the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM), leading to compilation failures and rendering the contract non-deployable and non-functional. This flaw not only disrupts the intended recovery mechanisms but also poses severe security risks if attempted to be exploited through unconventional means.

## Vulnerability Details

### **Proof of Concept (PoC)**

#### **1. Identification of Undefined Opcodes**

```solidity
assembly ("memory-safe") {
    tstore(owner, 1)
}
```

**Explanation:**  
The `tstore` opcode is used within an assembly block to store a value in a specific location. However, `tstore` is **not** a standard EVM opcode. The correct opcode for storing a value in storage is `sstore`. The use of `tstore` will result in a compilation error.

---

#### **2. Attempt to Load Undefined Opcode**

```solidity
assembly ("memory-safe") {
    valid := tload(recoveredAddress)
    if eq(valid, 1) { tstore(recoveredAddress, 0) }
}
```

**Explanation:**  
Similarly, `tload` is used to load a value from a specific location within an assembly block. `tload` is **not** a recognized EVM opcode. The standard opcode for loading a value from storage is `sload`. The presence of `tload` will cause the contract to fail during compilation.

---

#### **3. Compilation Failure Due to Undefined Opcodes**

```bash
Error: Undeclared identifier.
    tstore(owner, 1)
    ^^^^^
```

**Explanation:**  
When attempting to compile the `RecoverySpell.sol` contract, the Solidity compiler will throw an error indicating that `tstore` is an undeclared identifier. This prevents the contract from being successfully compiled and deployed.

---

#### **4. Hypothetical Scenario with Custom EVM Implementation**

```solidity
function executeRecovery() external {
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < owners.length; i++) {
        address owner = owners[i];
        assembly ("memory-safe") {
            tstore(owner, 1)
        }
    }
}
```

**Explanation:**  
If, hypothetically, a custom EVM implementation or preprocessor defines `tstore` and `tload`, the `executeRecovery` function could manipulate storage in unintended ways. This could allow unauthorized access or modification of critical variables, undermining the contract's security and integrity.

---

## Impact

- **Contract Deployment Failure:** The use of undefined opcodes `tstore` and `tload` prevents the `RecoverySpell.sol` contract from being compiled and deployed using standard Solidity compilers.
  
- **Security Risks:** If a custom EVM implementation were to interpret these undefined opcodes, it could lead to unauthorized storage manipulations, allowing malicious actors to alter critical contract state variables.
  
- **Operational Disruption:** The failure to deploy the `RecoverySpell` contract disrupts the recovery mechanisms of the Kleidi Wallet, potentially locking users out of their funds without a reliable recovery method.

## Tools Used


- **Manual Review** 

## Recommendations

1. **Remove Undefined Opcodes:**
   - **Eliminate `tstore` and `tload`:** Replace these with standard EVM opcodes such as `sstore` and `sload` for storage operations.
   
   ```solidity
   assembly {
       sstore(ownerSlot, 1)
   }
   ```
   
   **Explanation:**  
   Using `sstore` ensures that values are correctly stored in the designated storage slots, adhering to EVM standards.

# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept
background:
1. The protocol hopes to use pause to ensure the safety of funds when the safe wallet loses control. After the pause, the attacker cannot perform any operations through safe.
2. In the pause function, all proposals will be looped and deleted.
3. If an attacker obtains the safe wallet, [he can freely create proposals](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L521).

```solidity
        bytes32[] memory proposals = _liveProposals.values();
        for (uint256 i = 0; i < proposals.length; i++) {
            bytes32 id = proposals[i];

            delete timestamps[id];
            assert(_liveProposals.remove(id));

            emit Cancelled(id);
        }
```

Therefore, an attacker can continue to create proposals after gaining control of the safe wallet. Let the number of proposals be huge. Until the pause function is called, it fails because the gas exceeds the gas limit of the transaction. This prevents pausing.

If we calculate the gas consumption of the pause function, we can get:
• Remove timestamps[id]: ~5,000 gas.
• Remove _liveProposals.remove(id): Assume ~15,000 gas.
• Trigger event emit Canceled(id): about 631 gas.
• Base cost for other memory operations, array accesses, and control flow: approximately 1,000 gas.
• The total gas consumption per loop is roughly: 5000 + 15000 + 631 + 1000 = 21,631 gas
Assuming that the gas limit of a single transaction is 15,000,000 gas, using the previously estimated gas of 21,631 gas per cycle, we can calculate the approximate number of cycles ≈ 15,000,000 / 21,631 ≈ 693 times

Although the attacker needs to pay some gas cost. But if the amount of timelock funds is huge, then the effort is worth it.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
It is recommended not to include the operation of deleting proposals in pause. We can write another function for pause to call.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/RecoverySpell.sol#L118
https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/RecoverySpell.sol#L215


# Vulnerability details

### Proof Of Concept

The vulnerability exists in the constructor of the `RecoverySpell` contract, which allows the addition of any Ethereum addresses, including smart contract wallets, as owners. The issue arises during recovery when the signature verification process checks owners' signatures using the `ECDSA.recover` function, which is designed for EOA. 

We can read in the documentation:
>The protocol is opinionated and is designed to be used with Gnosis Safe multisigs

However, if one of the owners is a smart contract wallet (like a Gnosis Safe), signature verification should follow EIP-1271, which specifies how smart contracts should validate signatures. Since the current implementation does not account for smart contract wallets, this can cause invalid signature verification for such owners, potentially preventing legitimate recovery actions.

The constructor for `RecoverySpell` does not validate that the owners are regular EOA (Externally Owned Accounts). Safe wallets, for instance, allow smart contract wallets to act as owners, so a user may assume that the `RecoverySpell` works the same way.

```solidity
constructor(
    address[] memory _owners,
    address _safe,
    uint256 _safeThreshold,
    uint256 _recoveryThreshold,
    uint256 _delay
) {
    owners = _owners;
    safe = Safe(payable(_safe));
    threshold = _safeThreshold;
    recoveryThreshold = _recoveryThreshold;
    delay = _delay;

    recoveryInitiated = block.timestamp;

    emit RecoveryInitiated(block.timestamp, msg.sender);
}
```

In the recovery process, the signature is validated using the `ECDSA.recover` method:
```solidity
address recoveredAddress = ECDSA.recover(digest, v[i], r[i], s[i]);
```
This only works for EOAs, not smart contract wallets, which should use `isValidSignatureNow` from `SignatureChecker.sol` to account for smart contracts that implement EIP-1271.

The impact is that recovery attempts will fail if any of the `owners` is a smart contract wallet, as their signatures will not be correctly validated. This could leave users unable to recover control of their wallet in emergency situations if they have added smart contract wallets as owners.


### Recommended Mitigation Steps

To properly validate signatures from smart contract wallets and EOAs alike, the `SignatureChecker.sol` library from OpenZeppelin should be used. Specifically, the `isValidSignatureNow` function should replace the current `ECDSA.recover` mechanism to ensure compliance with EIP-1271.

This modification ensures that smart contract wallets, which implement EIP-1271, can also validate their signatures during the recovery process, making the system compatible with both EOAs and smart contract owners.

Moreover, I recommend to make sure that reentrancy is not possible since EIP-1271 involve external calls.




## Assessed type

DoS

https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L685-L700
https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L871-L934
https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L1028-L1155
https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L1189-L1243

# Vulnerability details


## Description

The use of `Bytes32Set.values()` in multiple state-changing functions could lead to a denial of service (DoS).

This operation copies the entire storage to memory, which is costly, especially when the set grows large.

Since it can become prohibitively expensive to call functions like `pause()`, `_addCalldataCheck()`, `removeCalldataCheckDatahash()`, `_removeCalldataCheck()` and `_removeAllCalldataChecks()`, it may render them uncallable.

This could result in situations where the pause guardian doesn't desire to pause the contract, or the timelock refuses/is-unable to manage calldatas due to high-gas-costs/exceeding-block-gaslimit.

Without setting a proper limits on the number of live proposals timelock can have or calldatas that can be stored per index range, there's possiblity of Denial of Service, that can happen.

Also we can take a look at function natspec of `values(Bytes32Set storage set)` inside the `EnumerableSet.sol`, where OZ has warned us about it: [#L211-L228](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/28aed34dc5e025e61ea0390c18cac875bfde1a78/contracts/utils/structs/EnumerableSet.sol#L211-L228)

```javascript
    /**
     * @dev Return the entire set in an array
     *
     * WARNING: This operation will copy the entire storage to memory, which can be quite expensive. This is designed
     * to mostly be used by view accessors that are queried without any gas fees. Developers should keep in mind that
     * this function has an unbounded cost, and using it as part of a state-changing function may render the function
     * uncallable if the set grows to a point where copying to memory consumes too much gas to fit in a block.
     */
    function values(Bytes32Set storage set) internal view returns (bytes32[] memory) {
        bytes32[] memory store = _values(set._inner);
        bytes32[] memory result;

        assembly ("memory-safe") {
            result := store
        }

        return result;
    }

```

## Impact

Expensive gas operations could prevent critical timelock functions from being executed. like pause guardian refusing/notHavingEnoughFunds to pause the contract due to very high gas cost incase of emergency or timelock refusing/is-unable to manage calldatas due to high-gas-cost/exceeding-block-gas-limit.

## Proof Of Concept

`Bytes32Set.values()` is used in functions below:

- Whenever [pause guardian pauses the contract](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L685-L700), we retrieve all live proposals with [_liveProposals.values()](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L691) and since this is a function that modifies state, retrieving large number of proposals can cause DOS.
  
- in dataHash removal process with [removeCalldataCheckDatahash()](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L871-L934), if dataHash we removed was the last dataHash that was stored in `dataHashes`, we [remove that index](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L903-L920) by replacing last index `startIndex`, `endIndex` and all stored `dataHashes` with current index that we just removed an dataHash from. we first retrieve last index associated with that function, [specifically we retrieve last index dataHashes and replace it's values with the current index that we just removed dataHash from](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L911C1-L916C14).  as you can see we have for loop that basically, loops through all dataHashes of last Index and stores it to current Index we just removed dataHash from, and then pop the last Index. effectively removing the Index that Has no dataHashes stored in it. if dataHashes stored in last Index is way to many, that can cause DOS.

- third accurance of `Bytes32Set.values()` is in [_addCalldataCheck()](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L1028-L1155) function when we [emit an event](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L1153). this function itself has complex logic and many for loops, so for that reason it already costs alot of gas to execute this function. plus we emit event with all dataHashes that is stored in [indexes[targetIndex].dataHashes.values()](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L1153). calling this function either will result in having very high gas cost or revert due to exceeding block gas limit, for that reason, most likely is vulnerable to DOS.

- the function that is most likely vulnerable to DOS is [_removeCalldataCheck()](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L1189-L1243), for [same reasons](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L1207-L1232) explained above.

- last function that `Bytes32Set.values()` is used in is, [_removeAllCalldataChecks()](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L1245-L1286), [where we delete every single indexes with their stored dataHashes](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L1262-L1282), which can be very gas expensive.

## Recommended mitigation

1. add two new state variables to Timelock called `maxLiveProposals` and `maxDataHashPerIndexRange`.

    on Timelock Deployment, user sets a custom limit on total number of proposals that can be stored in `_liveProposals` and total number of hashed calldatas that can be stored in  `_calldataList.dataHashes` for each function and index range to avoid unbounded growth and potential DOS.
    
2. refactor `_addCalldataCheck()` in a way that does not allow new calldatas being added, if already has reached it's max limit for that function, specific index range. 
   
3. refactor `_schedule()` in a way that does not allow scheduling a new proposal if already has reached it's max proposal limit. 
   
4. also add a setter function so safe will be able to change `maxLiveProposals` and `maxDataHashPerIndexRange`, if they intended to.
   keep in mind that a require statement should put in place for such function to ensure `_newMaxLiveProposals` is greater than or equal to total number of live proposals and `_newMaxDataHashPerIndexRange` is greater than or equal to total number of calldatas stored for that function specific index range.


## Assessed type

DoS

# Lines of code

https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L52
https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L264-L309
https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L759-L769


# Vulnerability details

## Description

In the `Timelock` contract, there is no check to ensure that the `hotSigners` are the same as the owners of the `safe`.

According to the comment on [#L:52](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L52), "only safe owners can execute whitelisted calldatas," but the constructor and the `grantRole()` functions do not verify that hot signers are also safe owners.

The separation of the `owners` array for the safe contract and the `hotSigners` array for the timelock contract introduces the risk that non-safe owners could be granted the `HOT_SIGNER_ROLE` and have ablity to execute whitelisted calldatas.

This weakens the intended security model of the system by allowing external or unauthorized addresses to gain the ability to execute privileged actions.

## Impact

Non-safe owners may be granted the `HOT_SIGNER_ROLE`, enabling them to execute whitelisted calldatas without being authorized.

## Proof of Concepts

- In [Timelock constructor](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L264-L309), hot signers are granted `HOT_SIGNER_ROLE`, without any checks to ensure they are also safe owners as it's stated in [#L:52](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L52).

- the safe `owners` array and `hotSigners` array [are separate](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/TimelockFactory.sol#L6-L18), and nothing ensures in [TimelockFactory](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/TimelockFactory.sol#L36-L55) that `owners[i] == hotsigner[i]` when Deploying Timelock.

- The [grantRole()](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L759-L769) function does not validate the `account` against the list of safe owners to ensure only safe owners can have `HOT_SIGNER_ROLE`, this allows an arbitrary address to be assigned `HOT_SIGNER_ROLE`, even if they may not be one of the safe owners.

## Recommended mitigation

- Add a check in the [Timelock constructor](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L271C5-L309) to ensure that the account we are assigning `HOT_SIGNER_ROLE` to, is one of the safe owners.
  
- remove `hotSigners` array from [DeploymentParams](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/TimelockFactory.sol#L11) struct as member and simply pass safe `owners` array on deployment of Timelock, to assign `HOT_SIGNER_ROLE` to each safe owner.
  
- add a check in `Timelock::grantRole()` function to ensure [account](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L763) is one of the current owners of safe.


## Assessed type

# Lines of code

https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L1028-L1155


# Vulnerability details

## Description

The `addCheckCalldata()` function in the `Timelock` contract, currently allows for the entire calldata to be arbitrary if wildcard is set. This poses a security risk, as malicious hot signers could take advantage of the wildcard for arbitrary function calls with harmful parameters in some scenarios.

instead the wildcard functionality should be implemented in a way that, Timelock allows certain parts of calldata related to a specific contract and function, to be arbitrary(wildcard) and certain parts of calldata have restrictions(whitelisted).

its true that safe owners should be extra cautious when choosing a function for granting wildcard to, but the way the wildcard functionality is implemented now, it simply allows the hot signer to input any arbitrary data to each parameter and there's no way for safe owners to grant a wildcard to only specific parameter of a function.

also seems like developer wanted to implement the wildcard functionality the way i described because if we take a look at [checkCalldata()](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L470-L504) function, specifically [this part](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L488-L493). we check if retrieved index has granted a wildcard or not, but developer hasn't noticed that he implemented wildcard functionality in a way that once a function is granted a wildcard, no more indexes can be added for that function because of [this part](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L1062-L1067) in [_addCalldataCheck()](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L1028-L1155).

## Impact

Once a function is granted wildcard access, it gives hot signers too much ability to act freely or even maliciously in some scenarios, if wildcard is granted to wrong function. This violates the principle of least privilege in security, enabling malicious or unexpected actions.

it's better that the wildcard functionality is implemented in such way, that if safe owners decided to grant wildcard access to specific part of calldata, they could, instead of allowing the whole calldata to arbitrary. also be able to restrict certain parts of calldata with whitelisting calldatas.

## Proof Of Concept

wildcard functionality is currently implemented this way:

* we can determine whether or not wildcard is set for a function, by checking first index struct of a function. specifically it's `startIndex` and `endIndex` values.
  if (`startIndex == endIndex` && `startIndex == 4` && `_calldataList[contractAddress][selector].length == 1`), it means wildcard is granted for that function. you can read [_addCalldataCheck()](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L1028-L1155) function, to understand wildcard functionality better, specifically [#L1058-L1078](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L1058-L1078).

* once wildcard is granted for a function, hot signer can execute that function with `executeWhitelisted()` or `executeWhitelistedBatch()` function with any arbitrary calldata, because [checkCalldata() for loop](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L488-L503), once it sees `startIndex` and `endIndex` are equal for first Index Struct, it stops calldata validation process and allows hotsigner proceed with arbitrary data.


## Recommended Mitigation

refactor `addCheckCalldata()` and other calldata related functions, in a way that timelock can grant/remove a wildcard to/from specific parts of calldata and restrict other parts by whitelisting calldata.


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L728-L755


# Vulnerability details

## Description

The [addCalldataCheck()](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L841-L855) and [removeCalldataCheck()](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L857-L869) functions allow the timelock to add and remove calldatas for different index ranges of functions.

However, this mechanism contains a vulnerability where hot signers can exploit non-whitelisted parameters in function calls.

For example, if the timelock adds calldata for specific index range of a function, covering only the first parameter of that function, the hot signer can send arbitrary data for the remaining parameters even if this is not how safe owners what planned to do.

Similarly, if timelock removes index range and calldatas of a function that covers specific parameter, hot signer can send arbitrary data for that parameter, once index range covering that parameter is removed.

## Impact

when timelock adds calldata or removes specific index range of a function, Hot signers gain ability to execute those functions with passing arbitrary values for parameters that do not have any coverage.

## Proof of Concept

1. **Add Calldata Example:**  
   
   the `addCalldataCheck()` function, whitelists multiple calldatas for single index range.

lets imagine we have `someFunc(address, uint256)` and timelock wants to whitelist both parameters, with `addCalldataCheck()` function.

   to do so:

   * to whitelist `address` parameter: the `startIndex == 4` and `endIndex == 36`, and calldata is `0x4838B106FCe9647Bdf1E7877BF73cE8B0BAD5f97`. 
   * to whitelist `uint256` parameter: the `startIndex == 37` and `endIndex == 68`, and calldata is `0xde0b6b3a7640000`(1e18 in decimal). 

   now keep in mind the `addCalldataCheck()` function, whitelists multiple calldatas for single index range meaning a single parameter (it can cover all parameters in a single index range, but that's not how it's recommended to be used on [#L1102-L1108](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L1102-L1108), since it reduces flexibility), that means safe is going to [schedule()](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L512-L539) two operations for Timelock, to be able to whitelist both of this calldatas for that function.

   now lets imagine safe did schedule operation for both of those calldatas, and now it's ready for execution. hot signer chooses to execute an operation that is responsible for whitelisting `address` parameter of `someFunc(address, uint256)`.

once this calldata is added for that function, hot signer ignores second operation and doesn't execute it (the operation that is responsible for whitelisting second parameter of `someFunc(address, uint256)`), and then executes the `someFunc(address, uint256)` function with passing arbitrary `uint256`. 


2. **Remove Calldata Example:**  
   
    lets imagine timelock has added calldatas for each paramter of `someFunc(address, uint256)` (keep in mind each parameter has different index range). now timelock decides to remove entire [Index struct](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L247-L255) that covers first parameter with `removeCalldataCheck()` function.

after removal, this means hot signer can execute `someFunc(address, uint256)` with passing arbitrary `address` for first parameter, when calling this function.


## Recommended Mitigation

maybe this is a design choice where, if certain parameters of a function, dont have restrictions set, it means hot signer can pass any arbitrary value for that parameter, but it's better to add a mapping inside the Timelock that `enables/disables` hot signer access to a function, even if calldatas are set for it.

with use of that mapping, all functions by default are `disabled`.

after Timelock adds a calldata for specific function, the safe owners review added calldatas and parts they haven't put any restrictions on, once reviewed, they decide to either cover new/same index range of that function by adding new calldatas or `enable` that function for hot signers use.

same can be applied when timelock wants to remove an entire index range from a function. first timelock disables the function and hot signers cannot call that function, until is re-enabled again. in the meantime, timelock removes an index range and safe owners review the parts they put restrictions and parts they haven't, and then they either decide to add/remove calldata for/from that function or `re-enable` that function so hot signers can use it again but with new restrictions.



## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L99-L100
https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L512-L539
https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L857-L869
https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L871-L934
https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L936-L952


# Vulnerability details

## Description

calldata removal related functions like [removeCalldataCheck()](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L857-L869), [removeCalldataCheckDatahash()](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L871-L934) and [removeAllCalldataChecks()](https://github.com/solidity-labs-io/kleidi/blob/0d72b6cb5725c1380212dc76257da96fcfacf22f/src/Timelock.sol#L936-L952), do not currently inherit the `onlySafe` modifier, instead they inherit `onlyTimelock` modifier.

This means that, if a malicious calldata is uncautiously added by safe owners through timelock, the Safe owners must wait for the minimum timelock delay before they can delete the calldata since they have to schedule an operation for Timelock for calldata removal.
During this waiting period, a hot signer could potentially use the malicious calldata to harm the system before the safe/timelock is able to act.

## Impact

In the event of a malicious or unintentional calldata addition due to safe owners carelessness, safe owners are unable to delete the calldata immediately due to the timelock's delay. This leaves the system exposed to potential exploitation by hot signers, who could use the calldata and cause harm to the system before it is removed.

## Proof of Concepts

1. A malicious calldata is added to the system uncautiously by safe owners through timelock with `addCalldataCheck()` function.
2. Safe owners schedule a operation to timelock to delete the calldata but they are forced to wait for the timelock delay.
3. During this waiting period, a hot signer exploits malicious calldata and cause harm to the system (e.g., by draining funds) by executing it with `executeWhitelisted()` function.

## Recommended mitigation

Ensure that all functions responsible for deleting calldata inherit the `onlySafe` modifier, allowing safe owners to delete potentially harmful calldatas immediately without waiting for the timelock delay. 

also introduce new process where calldatas must get approved by timelock after they get added. meaning hot signers cannot use those newly added calldatas until they're approved. this creates 2 step process for calldata authorization and enhances the security of Timelock.


## Assessed type

Other

# Vulnerability Details

## Impact

`RecoverySpell.sol` [states](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/RecoverySpell.sol#L95-L99) that it is of CRITICAL importance for the deployer to have recovery spells with the `delay` for the `recoverySpell` to become executable (hereafter referred to as `recoveryDelay`) shorter than the `delay` for a scheduled proposal to become executable in `Timelock.sol` (hereafter referred to as `timelockDelay`)

Even though it is only a comment, it says that the condition should be met by default and is basically a rule that should be followed, but that it is not possible to enforce that in the smart contracts.

This will make deployers to follow the comment's instructions. However, if the recovery spell is malicious, they will lose their safe.


## Proof of Concept

1. The attacker creates a recovery spell with `recoveryDelay = 10 days`.

2. The deployer creates a new system instance with the malicious recovery spell and a `timelockDelay` of `20 days`. He chooses this delay because of the comment that says it is of critical importance for the following to be true: `recoveryDelay < timelockDelay`.

3. The `recoveryDelay` runs out and the malicious recovery spell gets executed.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The timing constraints recommended to be used by the protocol are unsafe and the protocol needs to assess which timing constraints are not exploitable, if such timing constraints exist.

It should also be assessed whether it is possible to enforce the timing constraints in the smart contracts.


## Assessed type

Timing

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L687-L700
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L815-L820


# Vulnerability details

# Vulnerability Details

## Impact

The documentation states that when the cold signers of a safe are compromised, the pause guardian can pause the contract to cancel all malicious proposals, preventing them from being executed. After that, the recovery spell can be triggered to rotate the signing keys.

However, when the pause guardian calls `pause()`, a new pause guardian must be set by calling `setGuardian()`.
This can only be done by the Timelock, meaning the proposal to set a new guardian has to wait `x days` until it can be executed.
The waiting period is determined by the `delay` (hereafter referred to as `timelockDelay`) of the Timelock, which has a maximum of `30 days`.
Furthermore a proposal can only be scheduled after the `pauseDuration` has ended.

As a result, the contract may remain unprotected for at least `timelockDelay` if the pause guardian needs to pause the contract.

If the cold signers are compromised again during this time, there will be no way to stop them from executing malicious proposals, which will cause a user to lose his funds.


## Proof of Concept

The following values are chosen for the important variables:

```
timelockDelay = 5 days
delay of RecoverySpellA = 10 days
delay of RecoverySpellB = 10 days
pauseDuration = 11 days
```

It is important to note that the `delay` of the recovery spells does not have the same purpose as the `timelockDelay`.

1. The cold signers are compromised.

2. RecoverySpellA is created to rotate the signing keys.

3. The pause guardian calls `pause()` to cancel all proposals, including the malicious ones, and gets deleted.

4. After the `10 days`, `executeRecoverySpell()` gets called to rotate the signing keys.

5. The Safe schedules a new proposal to set a new guardian, which can be executed after the `5 days`.

6. The cold signers of the safe get compromised again before the `timelockDelay` is over and call `cancel()` to cancel the proposal to set a new guardian. They also schedule malicious proposals.

7. RecoverySpellB is created to rotate the signing keys.

8. As there is no guardian to pause the contract, the malicious proposals will be executed before the `delay` of RecoverySpellB runs out.


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider allowing a user to set multiple guardians.
It is important to make sure that this is compatible with the whole protocol.
Furthermore, it is insufficient to provide security measures that only work under the assumption of one compromise attempt.
While these are sufficient to protect against one \$5 wrench attack, they simply raise the cost to a two times \$5 wrench attack.
In particular it is not necessary to kidnap a user for `30 days`. It is sufficient to hit him with a \$5 wrench on two different days.


## Assessed type

MEV

# Vulnerability details

# Vulnerability Details

## Impact

To protect against malicious recovery spells, the documentation states that it is important to have a longer time delay on the recovery spells than the timelock. This way the safe can remove the recovery spell with a proposal before it becomes executable.

However, if the protocol had to be protected by the pause guardian because the safe keys were compromised, a malicious recovery spell will be executable before it can be removed.

The issue is not possible when there is only one recovery spell, but the protocol clearly aims to set up multiple recovery spells and by restricting oneself to one recovery spell there can be times when cold signer key loss can not be recovered.
So the issue is clearly present in live deployments and can not be explained away by the system configuration.

## Proof of Concept

Consider the following scenario:

```
timelockDelay = 5 days
pauseDuration = 15 days
RecoverySpellA delay = 10 days
malicious RecoverySpellM delay = 10 days
```

1. The cold signers are compromised.

2. RecoverySpellA gets created to rotate the signing keys.

3. The pause guardian calls `pause()` to cancel the malicious proposals the compromised cold signers scheduled.

4. One day later RecoverySpellM gets created as well.

5. The contract is paused for `15 days` which means that, among other things, it is not possible to schedule proposals.

6. `10 days` later RecoverySpellA gets executed to rotate the signing keys.

6. One more day later, the malicious recovery spell will be executed and the safe will be lost, as there is no protection by the safe keys.


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

While the contest documentation claims that the wallet can be protected against malicious recovery spells, the finding shows that this protection is limited.

It is not possible to make minor changes in such a way that the intended protection is achieved.

Instead, the protocol design as a whole needs to be reconsidered or at least the safety guarantees that the protocol aims for must be lowered.


## Assessed type

Context

# Vulnerability details

# Vulnerability Details

## Impact

When a transaction by the safe is made, it is checked by `checkTransaction()` in `Guard.sol` that it is no self or delegate call so that no new modules, upgrades, owners or fallback handlers can be added or removed by the transaction.

It only allows self or delegate calls if the calldata is empty.

However, compromised signers of the safe could still make the safe call itself with non-empty calldata by using `Safe.handlePayment()`.

This means the invariant that the safe can only call itself with empty calldata is broken.

If the safe is configured in such a way that its security relies on that invariant (for example with fallback handler) then it is possible that an attack can be performed.

## Proof of Concept

1. The compromised signers make a transaction using `execTransaction()`.

2. They provide the address of the safe as the `gasToken`.

3. The guard will not revert the transaction, because it is not called when `handlePayment()` is executed.

4. `fallback()` will be called, which causes the fallback handler to be called when it is configured.

5. An attack could be performed due to the broken invariant.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider adding a check in `Guard.sol` that the `gasToken` is not the safe.

External contract logic that wants to create and execute the recovery spell in one transaction will not work.

```diff
require(
-    block.timestamp > recoveryInitiated + delay,
    "RecoverySpell: Recovery not ready"
);

require(
+    block.timestamp >= recoveryInitiated + delay,
    "RecoverySpell: Recovery not ready"
);
```

# Vulnerability details

# Vulnerability Details

## Impact

When a hot signer calls `executeWhitelisted()` or `executeWhitelistedBatch()`, `checkcalldata()` is executed to check the `payload` that he provided.
Inside this function, the calldata is checked to determine whether it is whitelisted.

It is documented that dynamic calldata, such as arrays, cannot be checked because parameters can be at unpredictable indexes depending on the array length. It is also stated that all supported protocols will have fixed-size calldata, so this is not a concern.

However, a compromised hot signer could execute whitelisted calldata to a whitelisted contract with excessive calldata by simply appending data to the whitelisted calldata.
This could alter the execution of the function specified by the calldata.

## Proof of Concept

Consider this function which would be vulnerable even though the formal function paramter contains no array:

```solidity
function transfer(uint amount) public view returns (uint res) {
    assembly {
        res := calldataload(36)
    }
    return res;
}
```

The following scenario is possible if the above function is whitelisted:

1. A hot signer is compromised

2. He calls `executeWhitelisted()` with the whitelisted calldata for the function but appends additional calldata at the end.

3. The function is executed, but it executes unexpected logic (for example it could transfer too much funds or interact with a defi protocol in an unexpected way), as the timelock does not check the length of the calldata.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider adding an option to set a size limit for the calldata when it is whitelisted.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L687-L700


# Vulnerability details

# Vulnerability Details

## Impact

When the cold signers are compromised, the pause guardian calls `pause()` to cancel all malicious proposals.

By doing that, he loops over every `_liveProposal` to delete it.
This means that `pause()` will run out of gas and therefore revert, if the malicious cold signers schedule too many proposals before the pause guardian pauses.

Therefore, the contract can not be paused and the malicious proposals can be executed before the recovery spell can rotate the signing keys.

It is THE main property of a kleidi wallet that compromised cold signers can not take over the safe.

## Proof of Concept

The following test should be added to `Timelock.t.sol`:

```solidity
function testPauseDoS() public {

    for (uint256 i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
        vm.prank(address(safe));
        timelock.schedule(
        address(timelock),
        0,
        abi.encodeWithSelector(timelock.updateDelay.selector, 30 days),
        bytes32(i),
        MINIMUM_DELAY
    );
    }

    vm.prank(guardian);
    timelock.pause();
}
```
This test schedules `10000` proposals and calls `pause()` afterwards.

Furthermore, a few lines need to be added in `Timelock.sol`:

```solidity
function pause() public override {
    /// check that msg.sender is the pause guardian, pause the contract
    super.pause();

+    console.log(gasleft());

    bytes32[] memory proposals = _liveProposals.values();
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < proposals.length; i++) {
        bytes32 id = proposals[i];

        delete timestamps[id];
        assert(_liveProposals.remove(id));

        emit Cancelled(id);
    }
+    console.log(gasleft());
}
```

Additionally, this import needs to be added on top of `Timelock.sol`:

```solidity
import {console} from "forge-std/console.sol";
```

The block gas limit on ethereum equals `30 Million` which means that any transaction that costs more gas than this will revert.
When running `forge test --mt testPauseDoS -vv` the following logs will be printed:

```
Ran 1 test for test/unit/Timelock.t.sol:TimelockUnitTest
[PASS] testPauseDoS() (gas: 1560418624)
Logs:
  18158513696823674292
  18158513696791425309

Suite result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 skipped; finished in 1.17s (1.16s CPU time)

Ran 1 test suite in 1.19s (1.17s CPU time): 1 tests passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped (1 total tests)
```
The first log equals the result of the `gasleft()` function call before entering the loop.
The second log equals the result of the `gasleft()` function call after the loop, which means all proposals have been deleted.

This means that the difference of both numbers is the amount of gas that has been used by deleting every proposal. Said difference is:
`18158513696823674292 - 18158513696791425309 = 32248983`, which is higher than `30 Million`.

Taking this into account, the following scenario becomes possible:

```
timelockDelay = 2 days
delay of RecoverySpellA = 5 days
pauseDuration = 6 days
```

1. The cold signers are compromised

2. They schedule `10000` proposals to flood `_liveProposals`

3. RecoverySpellA gets created to rotate the signing keys.

4. The pause guardian calls `pause()`, as he wants to cancel all malicious proposals and buy time until the recovery spell becomes executable

5. `pause()` reverts as it reaches the block gas limit

6. After `2 days` the malicious proposals become executable and the safe is lost.


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider adding a limit to the amount of proposals that can be live at the same time.








## Assessed type

DoS

# Vulnerability details

# Vulnerability Details

## Impact

When a hot signer calls `executeWHitelisted()` or `executeWhitelistedBatch()` to execute a call to whitelisted contracts with whitelisted calldatas, he can provide one or more `values`, depending on which of the said functions he calls.

The `value` will be sent to the provided `target`, if `checkCalldata()` does not revert.

However, there is no validation that checks the amount of funds he provided.
This means that any hot signer can call this function and send any amount to a whitelisted contract and therefore drain the contract, as the timelock is the address that holds all funds.

The risk is definitely real, as the functions are payable and therefore suggest that it is intended use to have targets and selectors that allow `msg.value` to be passed.

Furtermore, `Timelock.sol` has a `receive()` function, which means that it is expected to receive and hold native funds.

## Proof of Concept

1. The calls that can be made by calling `executeWHitelisted()` or `executeWhitelistedBatch()` first need to be whitelisted. 

2. This can be done either when the system instance is created when `createSystemInstance()` in `InstanceDeployer.sol` gets called or when the timelock calls `addCalldataCheck()` or `addCalldataChecks()` in `Timelock.sol`, which can be done when a proposal that has been scheduled by the safe is executed.

3. Any hot signer can call `executeWhitelisted()` or `executeWhitelistedBatch()` to execute any of those whitelisted calls with any `value`.

4. This could be done anytime by any hot signer with any `value` until the contract has been drained.


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

For each (contract,selector) pair the maximum amount should also be whitelisted.

An alternative solution, if the timelock is not expected to hold ETH, is to not allow `executeWhitelisted()` and `executeWhitelistedBatch()` to access any funds in excess of `msg.value` that has been provided by the hot signer.

# Vulnerability details

The `_paramChecks` function in the `RecoverySpellFactory` contract incorrectly validates the maximum allowed `delay` for recovery operations. It assumes a year always consists of 365 days, failing to account for leap years. This can lead to unexpected transaction reverts when attempting to set a delay that includes February 29th in a leap year.

This bug affects the createRecoverySpell and calculateAddress functions, as they rely on _paramChecks for parameter validation.

## Steps to Reproduce

1.  Use the `createRecoverySpell` function in a leap year (e.g., 2024).
2.  Provide a `delay` value that equates to 366 days or more (including February 29th).
3.  The transaction will revert with the error "RecoverySpell: Delay must be lte a year."

## Expected Result

The transaction should succeed as long as the provided `delay` is within one year from the current date, correctly accounting for leap years.

## Actual Result

The transaction reverts due to the inaccurate calculation of the maximum allowed delay.

## Vulnerability Details

The following line in the `_paramChecks` function causes the issue:

```solidity
require(delay <= 365 days, "RecoverySpell: Delay must be lte a year"); 
```

This hardcoded value of `365 days` does not adapt to leap years.

## Impact

This bug affects users who need to set recovery delays that span across leap years. It can disrupt the intended functionality of the contract and lead to confusion.

## Proposed Solution

1.  **Calculate the exact timestamp one year from now**:

    uint256 oneYearFromNow = block.timestamp + 365 days; 
    // Add an extra day if the current year is a leap year
    if ((block.timestamp % 4 == 0 && block.timestamp % 100 != 0) || block.timestamp % 400 == 0) {
        oneYearFromNow += 1 days;
    }
    require(delay <= oneYearFromNow, "RecoverySpell: Delay must be lte a year");

# Vulnerability details

## Describtion
The contract `RecoverySpell` is deployed with an array of new owners. This array is used when recovery is executed and new owners are set. However there is an edge case scenario which causes revert of the function `executeRecovery`.

#### Example scenario:
We have 3/4 multisig. And one of the signers is another multisig. 
This wallet is considered safe and thats why we include the wallet to the recovery owners array. Other addresses will be new.

Threshold is set to 3/4 and 2 signer keys are lost. So we have the following list of Safe owners

```
# L - Lost key
# M - multisig
og = [A_L, B_L, C, D_M]
```

and a set of new recovery owners:

```
new = [D_M, E, F, G]
```

And we execute recovery process.

Now if we follow the code
* _remove all but final existing owner, set owner threshold to 1_

state after `OwnerManager.removeOwner` calls
```
og = [D_M]
```

* _swap final existing owner for the first new owner_

and **here** is the problem. Swapping `[existingOwners[existingOwnersLength - 1]` for `owners[0]`
Aka **Swapping D_M for D_M**.

We can see in Safe `OwnerManager` contract:

```solidity
    function swapOwner(address prevOwner, address oldOwner, address newOwner) public authorized {
        // Owner address cannot be null, the sentinel or the Safe itself.
        require(newOwner != address(0) && newOwner != SENTINEL_OWNERS && newOwner != address(this), "GS203");
        // No duplicate owners allowed.
        require(owners[newOwner] == address(0), "GS204");
        // Validate oldOwner address and check that it corresponds to owner index.
        require(oldOwner != address(0) && oldOwner != SENTINEL_OWNERS, "GS203");
        require(owners[prevOwner] == oldOwner, "GS205");
        owners[newOwner] = owners[oldOwner];
        owners[prevOwner] = newOwner;
        owners[oldOwner] = address(0);
        emit RemovedOwner(oldOwner);
        emit AddedOwner(newOwner);
    }
```

More specifically:

```solidity
require(owners[newOwner] == address(0), "GS204");
```

The address `D_M` was not removed before, and it is the last address remaining. It does point to `SENTINEL_OWNERS`.

It is an edge scenario, but the impact is very dangerous as it will make the recovery permanently DoSed. The system should be robust enough for all different use-cases, including the mentioned one.

## PoC

See Safe test - same address swap fail:
https://github.com/safe-global/safe-smart-account/blob/6fde75d29c8b52d5ac0c93a6fb7631d434b64119/test/core/Safe.OwnerManager.spec.ts#L313C1-L322C12

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
In case any address will be re-used for a new owner set, make sure it does not occupy the zero index of recovery owners

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L443-L450
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L429-L436


# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept
`Timelock` contracts do not implement `EIP712` correctly.

According to [EIP712 Standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-712#definition-of-typed-structured-data-%F0%9D%95%8A):

> The dynamic values `bytes` and `string` are encoded as a `keccak256` hash of their contents.

However, in [`Timelock:hashOperation()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L429-L436) and [`Timelock:hashOperationBatch()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L443-L450), the hashing is done as follows:
```solidity
    function hashOperation(
        address target,
        uint256 value,
>>      bytes calldata data, // bytes
        bytes32 salt
    ) public pure returns (bytes32) {
>>      return keccak256(abi.encode(target, value, data, salt)); // encoded & hashed directly
    }

    function hashOperationBatch(
        address[] calldata targets,
        uint256[] calldata values,
>>      bytes[] calldata payloads, // bytes
        bytes32 salt
    ) public pure returns (bytes32) {
>>      return keccak256(abi.encode(targets, values, payloads, salt)); // encoded & hashed directly
    }
```
As seen, both `data` and `payloads` are `bytes` values. However, the hashing encodes these values directly and not the `keccak256` hash of their contents as required by the standard.

**Affected functions**:
1. [`schedule()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L528)
2. [`scheduleBatch()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L562)
3. [`execute()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L595)
4. [`executeBatch()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L632)

## Impact
---> Non-compliance with `EIP712` can cause problems with integrators and potentially lead to denial of service.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Correct this as follows:
```diff
    // hashOperation()
-   return keccak256(abi.encode(target, value, data, salt));
+   return keccak256(abi.encode(target, value, keccak256(data), salt));

    // hashOperationBatch()
-   return keccak256(abi.encode(targets, values, payloads, salt));
+   return keccak256(abi.encode(targets, values, keccak256(payloads), salt));
```








## Assessed type

Other
