This is likely to be a contentious issue, so the reviewer will deviate from the usual submission template to make a clear case for this issue.

The birthday paradox refers to the counterintuitive fact that in a room of only 23 people there is a probability exceeding 50% that any two people share a birthday.

ELI5 (as much for my own benefit as for the reader’s.)

Where there are random numbers generated, there is a much greater likelihood that there will be any number that is drawn at least twice, than a single predetermined number. In other words, for a set of 0 <= x <= 99 possible numbers, if we only make 10 draws (and not excluding this number from subsequent draws) looking for the number x, then there is for each draw a 0.01 probability to get x, and so for a sample of 10 draws the probability of finding x is 0.1.

But, the chance of drawing any two values that are the same, in those 10 draws is about 0.39. For 25 draws the odds are about 0.95. See more about this calculation and this attack vector here.

Hashing
For the keccak256 hashing used in the EVM, it means that there are 2^256 possible hashes for all possible inputs. Of course, all the possible inputs are much greater than 2^256. This brings us to the pigeonhole problem (which we run into when we cast values from uint256 to uint64, as an example). To simplify, where there are functions that have a greater number of valid inputs than the number possible outcomes, then logically there must be multiple inputs that have the same output.

function calculateCreate2Address(
    address creator,
    bytes memory creationCode,
    bytes memory constructorParams,
    bytes32 salt
) pure returns (address) {
    return address(
        uint160(
            uint256(
                keccak256(
                    abi.encodePacked(
                        bytes1(0xff),
                        creator,
                        salt,
                        keccak256(
                            abi.encodePacked(creationCode, constructorParams)
                        )
                    )
                )
            )
        )
    );
}

function calculateCreate2Address(Create2Params memory params)
    pure
    returns (address)
{
    return address(
        uint160(
            uint256(
                keccak256(
                    abi.encodePacked(
                        bytes1(0xff),
                        params.creator,
                        params.salt,
                        keccak256(
                            abi.encodePacked(
                                params.creationCode, params.constructorParams
                            )
                        )
                    )
                )
            )
        )
    );
}


We know that keccak256 provides a 256-bit result, but then that 256-bit result is truncated to a 160-bit value. The preceeding 96-bit value is lost. Meaning that for every 160-bit address derived by the code above, there would have been 2^96 possible values that could have led to that address. For our N of 160, this means an attacker would need to compute sqrt(2^160), which is 2^80, to be likely to find a collision.


Proof of Concept
Consider the following:

There are 2^160 possible EVM addresses.
There are 2^256 possible hash outputs for the keccak256 function.
Therefore, there must be hash outputs where the last 160 bits of the 256 bit hash output are the same. There are 2^96 different keccak256 hash outputs that would share the same last 160 bits.

The odds of person creating an address using counterfactual deployment (or normal EOA generation) and so create an account with the same address as a specific target address in normal on-chain use are so small that it’s practically impossible.

But the probability of getting a usable address from address deployment is the probability of ANY address derived using the method in the validateCallback function being the same as ANY address (EOA or deterministic) derived by the attacker through some seed values. This greatly reduces the amount of compute necessary, but it is still not trivial.

The attacker would need to compute at least two sets of 2^80 - one set for the EOA and the other for the combination of PoolFeatures that would clash. With that there is a 39% chance of a clash.

As the submission by 0x52 showed, drawing 2^81 samples would raise the success rate to 86%.

A note on feasibility
As the feasibility of this attack is probably the greatest limiting factor, it would be wise to get some real-world bounds for this.

Please note that these are rough estimates to provide context

Some Antminers can reach 255 terahashes/second.
It costs around USD 4200 for one such machine.
It has an energy requirement of 5.4kW.
Per the above there would need to be at least two sets of 2^81 hashes.
Given these parameters it would take a single antminer (at 255Th/s) about 300 years to generate the first set. (2^81 hashes at 255e12 hashes generated per second). So to do it in one year would require about 300 antminers, thus a capital outlay of USD 1.26 million. Then you need the second set, so it would take another year for a total of two sets. In terms of power you would need 5.4kw (single machine power draw) * 300 (number of miners) * 0.12 (cost per kwh) * 8784 (hours in a year) * 2 (using the average cost to businesses of 0.12 USD per kWh), which gives about USD 3,415,219.2 of energy costs in total.

## Proof of Concept

The InstanceDeployer.sol contract uses IMulticall3.aggregate3 with Enum.Operation.DelegateCall to batch multiple operations, including adding owners and enabling modules on the Gnosis Safe.

Delegate calls are risky because they allow external contracts to execute code in the context of the calling contract, potentially leading to storage corruption or reentrancy attacks. If any malicious recovery spells or modules are added during the multicall, they can exploit this delegate call to manipulate storage or reenter critical functions.

```
require(
    Safe(payable(walletInstance.safe)).execTransaction(
        multicall3,
        0,
        abi.encodeWithSelector(IMulticall3.aggregate3.selector, calls3),
        Enum.Operation.DelegateCall,
        0,
        0,
        0,
        address(0),
        payable(0),
        signature
    ),
    "InstanceDeployer: Safe delegate call failed"
);
```
An attacker adds a malicious recovery spell during the multicall. The spell’s code is executed in the context of the Safe due to the delegateCall. As a result, it can corrupt storage, modify the Safe's owners, or execute unauthorized code.
Additionally, the delegate call could open the door to reentrancy attacks, especially if one of the contracts called during the multicall interacts with external systems.

Storage Corruption: If the delegate call executes code from an external contract with a different storage layout, it can overwrite critical state variables, potentially causing unauthorized access or loss of control over the Safe.
Reentrancy Attacks: Delegate calls allow contracts to execute in the caller’s context, which can lead to reentrancy vulnerabilities if not properly guarded. An attacker could exploit reentrant behavior to gain unauthorized control or funds.




## Recommended Mitigation Steps


Avoid delegateCall Where Possible:
Use direct calls (Enum.Operation.Call) to avoid storage corruption or malicious code execution.
Replace the delegateCall operation with a regular call:

```

require(
    Safe(payable(walletInstance.safe)).execTransaction(
        multicall3,
        0,
        abi.encodeWithSelector(IMulticall3.aggregate3.selector, calls3),
        Enum.Operation.Call,  // Replace DelegateCall with Call
        0,
        0,
        0,
        address(0),
        payable(0),
        signature
    ),
    "InstanceDeployer: Safe call failed"
);
```

Ensure all modules and recovery spells being added are validated and trusted. This can be done by using a whitelist or requiring security audits for all modules and contracts involved in the multicall.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L1119-L1124


# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept

Due to an invalid check of `startIndex` and `endIndex`, parameters for the functionSelectors cannot be added to the `callDataCheck.dataHash` correctly.

lets say ,  safe wants to whiteList `mul2numbers(bytes2 x,bytes2 y)` from a contract `Multiply` so that hot signers can execute mul operations from `timelock`.

safe will schedule an operation to add this `callDatacheck` so that when the operation is ready to execute, `timeLock` can execute `addCallDataCheck` (a user will be callling execute() to execute this operation).

```solidity
timelock.addCalldataCheck(
        contractAddress, selector, startIndex, endIndex, datas
);
```

Now to whitelist a `bytes2` value `(hex("1234"))` for the parameter `x` , the inputs datas passed would be
```
    contractAddress : address(`Multiply`)
    selector : timelock.addCalldataCheck.selector,
    startIndex:4
    endIndex:6
    datas:hex("1234")
```

and then safe decided to whitelist another bytes2 value (hex("1234")) for the parameter `y` , here the inputs datas passed would be
```
    contractAddress : address(`Multiply`)
    selector : timelock.addCalldataCheck.selector,
    startIndex:6
    endIndex:8
    datas:hex("3456")
```
This should efficiently store both these parameters inside the callDataChecks since

   ` hex(1234)` will occupy the `callDatas`'s  ` 4th index` and `5th index` (total occupying 2 bytes spaces) and
    `hex(3456)` will occupy the `callDatas`'s  `6th index` and `8th index` (total occupying 2 bytes spaces)

>There shouldnot not be any overlap.

But,
due to the [check](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L1119-L1123) in the `_addCalldataCheck()` 

```solidity
    require(
        startIndex > indexes[i].endIndex
            || endIndex < indexes[i].startIndex,
        "CalldataList: Partial check overlap"
    );
            
```
It will always revert.

>`startIndex` can equal to `endIndex` of newly added callDataCheck since while adding a callData value into a callDataCheck , it will only occupy from `startIndex` to `endIndex - 1` of it.


### POC
forge test --match-test testDCantAddDatastoCallDataCheck -vvv

```solidity
    function testDCantAddDatastoCallDataCheck() public {
        bytes[] memory datasX = new bytes[](1);
        datasX[0] = hex"1234"; //it is a 2 bytes long data

        vm.prank(address(timelock));
        timelock.addCalldataCheck(
            address(10000), timelock.addCalldataCheck.selector, 4, 6, datasX
        ); //occupy 4th and 5th index

        bytes[] memory datasY = new bytes[](1);
        datasY[0] = hex"3456"; //it is a 2 bytes long data
        vm.prank(address(timelock));
        vm.expectRevert("CalldataList: Partial check overlap"); // It will revert with this message 
        timelock.addCalldataCheck(
            address(10000), timelock.addCalldataCheck.selector, 6, 8, datasY
        ); //should occupy 6th and 7th index but it will revert
    }
```
when adding the datasY , the addCalldataCheck will revert.

## Impact

The safe cannot whitelist callDatachecks for functions with more than 1 parameters.


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
```solidity
    require(
        startIndex >= indexes[i].endIndex
            || endIndex <= indexes[i].startIndex,
        "CalldataList: Partial check overlap"
    );
            
```

## Proof of Concept

Safe can schedule different operations so that after the required delay those operation can be executed by anyone.

These operations typically involve timelock functions, enabling Safe owners to update the state variables of the timelock.

However, this setup could lead to an undesirable scenario:

1. `Safe` owners may decide to use `removeCalldataChecks()` to remove all `callDataChecks` from a function of a `target contract`, followed by using `addCallDataChecks()` to add new `callDataChecks` in the same block. 3. Once the delay has passed and both operations are ready for execution, an `attacker` could `frontrun` the execution by ensuring that `addCallDataChecks()` is executed first. They could then choose whether or not to execute `removeCallDataChecks()` afterward.

This would force the `Safe` owners to `reschedule` the `addCallDataChecks()`, potentially leading to significant losses as they may fail to secure funds from a protocol in time.

This vulnerability could have severe consequences for Safe owners, such as losing control over funds.

# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept
The `cancel` function in Timelock contract allows cancellation of an operation without checking if it has already been executed. It only checks if the operation exists and is in the `_liveProposals` set. As a result, even executed operations can be cancelled, effectively "un-executing" them in the contract's state.

Operations that have been executed can appear as pending or non-existent. Cancelled operations could potentially be re-executed. 

Consider the following sequence of events

1. An operation with ID `x` is scheduled.
2. The operation is executed, setting `timestamps[x] = 1` (DONE_TIMESTAMP).
3. The `cancel(x)` function is called, which succeeds.
4. The cancellation removes `x` from `_liveProposals` and sets `timestamps[x] = 0`.
5. Now, `isOperation(x)` returns true (because `timestamps[x] = 0`), but the operation has been executed.

In the [Timelock contract:#L657-L665](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L657-L665)
```solidity
function cancel(bytes32 id) external onlySafe whenNotPaused {
    require(
        isOperation(id) && _liveProposals.remove(id),
        "Timelock: operation does not exist"
    );

    delete timestamps[id]; // <= FOUND
    emit Cancelled(id);
}
```
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Implement a check in the cancel function to ensure that only non-executed operations can be cancelled.
```diff
function cancel(bytes32 id) external onlySafe whenNotPaused {
    require(
-       isOperation(id) && _liveProposals.remove(id),
+       isOperation(id) && !isOperationDone(id) && _liveProposals.remove(id),
        "Timelock: operation does not exist or is already executed"
    );

    delete timestamps[id];
    emit Cancelled(id);
}
```

# Vulnerability details

Timelock contract's `executeWhitelisted` function contains a flaw due to insufficient validation of input data. This function, intended to allow trusted signers to execute whitelisted actions, fails to properly validate the entire calldata, potentially allowing malicious transactions to bypass security checks.

Why it happened is because the `checkCalldata` function, called within `executeWhitelisted`, does not validate the entire payload. It likely only checks specific segments of the calldata, allowing carefully crafted malicious payloads to pass through undetected.
```solidity
function executeWhitelisted(
    address target,
    uint256 value,
    bytes calldata payload
) external payable onlyRole(HOT_SIGNER_ROLE) whenNotPaused {
    checkCalldata(target, payload);  // <= FOUND
    _execute(target, value, payload);
    emit CallExecuted(bytes32(0), 0, target, value, payload);
}
```
_The `checkCalldata` function's implementation likely focuses on validating specific parts of the payload, such as function selectors or certain parameters, without ensuring the integrity of the entire calldata. This partial validation creates a security gap that can be exploited._

1. Assume a whitelisted function `transfer(address,uint256)` on a target contract.
2. Create a malicious payload that appears to call `transfer` but actually contains additional data to execute an unauthorized action.
3. Call `executeWhitelisted` with:

   * `target`: The address of the whitelisted contract
   * `value`: 0
   * `payload`: The malicious payload

The `checkCalldata` function will pass this payload as valid, and `_execute` will process it.

## Proof of Concept
Consider a scenario where a whitelisted function `transfer(address,uint256)` exists on a target contract. An attacker with the HOT_SIGNER_ROLE could craft a malicious payload that appears to call `transfer` but contains additional data to execute an unauthorized action.

1. Attacker crafts a payload: `transfer(address,uint256) + malicious_data`
2. Attacker calls `executeWhitelisted(target, 0, malicious_payload)`
3. `checkCalldata` validates only the initial part of the payload, passing the check
4. `_execute` processes the entire payload, including the malicious part

We can see in this POC how partial validation in `checkCalldata` can be exploited to execute unauthorized actions through the timelock.

Enhance `checkCalldata` to validate the entire payload

                    calldataCheck.startIndex, calldataCheck.endIndex

        );

}

# Vulnerability details

`Timelock.cancel` function fails to update the `totalOperations` counter when an operation is cancelled, leading to a state inconsistency between the actual number of live operations and the recorded total.

This's an issue because the `cancel` function only removes the operation from the `_liveProposals` set and deletes its timestamp, without decrementing the `totalOperations` counter. This causes the counter to remain unchanged even when operations are cancelled, gradually increasing the discrepancy between the reported and actual number of live operations.

1. The issue s in the `cancel` function of the Timelock contract.
2. The `cancel` function is called with a valid operation ID.
3. The operation is successfully cancelled, removing it from the `_liveProposals` set.
4. However, the `totalOperations` counter is not properly updated.

## Proof of Concept
```solidity
function cancel(bytes32 id) external onlySafe whenNotPaused {
    require(
        isOperation(id) && _liveProposals.remove(id),
        "Timelock: operation does not exist"
    );

    delete timestamps[id];
    emit Cancelled(id); // <= FOUND
}
```
1. Schedule multiple operations (e.g., 5)
2. Verify `totalOperations` is 5
3. Cancel 2 operations using `cancel`
4. Check `totalOperations` - it will still be 5
5. Verify `getAllProposals().length` returns 3
6. Observe the discrepancy between `totalOperations` (5) and actual live operations (3)

This sequence of events clearly shows how the contract state becomes inconsistent after cancelling operations. In a governance context, this could lead to incorrect quorum or voting power calculations if they depend on the total number of operations.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Decrement the `totalOperations` counter when an operation is cancelled. 
```diff
    );

    delete timestamps[id];
+   totalOperations--;
    emit Cancelled(id);
}
```
Additionally, i'll recommend:

1. Add a function to reconcile `totalOperations` with the actual number of live operations, in case discrepancies have already occurred.
2. Implement periodic checks to ensure `totalOperations` matches `_liveProposals.length()`.
3. Consider adding events to log changes in `totalOperations` for better off-chain tracking

# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept

This vulnerability arises from a combination of reentrancy issues in InstanceDeployer.createSystemInstance() and RecoverySpell.executeRecovery(), alongside ignored return values in AccessControlEnumerable._grantRole() and _revokeRole(). Together, these flaws enable an attacker to use reentrancy to repeatedly bypass role checks and alter access control state, granting or maintaining unauthorized privileges. The lack of return value checks allows roles to persist despite intended removals, giving an attacker prolonged and unrestricted access to privileged functions.

### Impact
An attacker could exploit this vulnerability to establish and maintain unauthorized roles, granting themselves high-level privileges. This could lead to unrestricted access to critical functions, including unauthorized system instance creation and recovery disruptions, resulting in significant compromise of the contract’s security and integrity.

### Scenario

'''solidity

// Reentrant attack with createSystemInstance or executeRecovery
safeProxy = SafeProxyFactory(safeProxyFactory).createProxyWithNonce(...);
walletInstance.timelock = Timelock(...);
// Reentrant access to _grantRole and _revokeRole
for (uint256 i = 0; i < reentrantCalls; i++) {
    _grantRole(adminRole, attacker); // Return value ignored, attacker gains admin role
    _revokeRole(adminRole, legitimateUser); // Return value ignored, legitimate user loses admin role
}
emit SystemInstanceCreated(...); // Event emitted after reentrancy
'''

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L657-L665

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/test/unit/Timelock.t.sol#L1193-L1213


# Vulnerability details

When cancelling an operation

1. The proposal is removed from `_liveProposals`
2. `timestamps[id]` is deleted (set to 0)
3. A subsequent execution could still pass the `isOperationReady()` check if the timestamps and expiration period align correctly

The vulnerability stems from improper invalidation of cancelled operations. When an operation is cancelled, its timestamp is set to 0 using `delete`. However, the `isOperationReady()` check can still pass with a timestamp of 0 due to how the arithmetic conditions are structured, allowing cancelled operations to be re-executed if timed correctly.

The issue occurs in the following sequence

1. Safe schedules an operation, setting:

   * `timestamps[id]` = future timestamp
   * `_liveProposals` contains operation id

2. Safe cancels the operation:

   * Removes from `_liveProposals`
   * Sets timestamps[id] to 0 via delete

3. Attacker executes cancelled operation:

   * If `block.timestamp < expirationPeriod`
   * `isOperationReady()` passes despite cancellation
   * Operation executes successfully

[src/Timelock.sol#cancel](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L657-L665)
[src/Timelock.sol#isOperationReady](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L399-L404)
[src/Timelock.sol#execute](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L589-L609)
```solidity
function cancel(bytes32 id) external onlySafe whenNotPaused {
    require(
        isOperation(id) && _liveProposals.remove(id),
        "Timelock: operation does not exist"
    );

    delete timestamps[id]; // <@audit Sets to 0 instead of invalidating // Using delete sets to 0 which can pass isOperationReady() check
    emit Cancelled(id);
}

function isOperationReady(bytes32 id) public view returns (bool) {
    uint256 timestamp = timestamps[id];
    return timestamp > _DONE_TIMESTAMP && timestamp <= block.timestamp // <@audit: Can pass with timestamp 0 // Cancelled ops with timestamp 0 can pass this check
        && timestamp + expirationPeriod > block.timestamp;
}

function execute(
    address target,
    uint256 value,
    bytes calldata payload,
    bytes32 salt
) external payable whenNotPaused {
    bytes32 id = hashOperation(target, value, payload, salt);

    require(_liveProposals.remove(id), "Timelock: proposal does not exist"); // <@audit First check
    require(isOperationReady(id), "Timelock: operation is not ready"); // <@audit Second check can pass for cancelled ops

    _execute(target, value, payload);
    emit CallExecuted(id, 0, target, value, payload);

    _afterCall(id);
}
```
[test/unit/Timelock.t.sol#testCancelActiveProposalSafeSucceeds](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/test/unit/Timelock.t.sol#L1193-L1213)
```solidity
function testCancelActiveProposalSafeSucceeds() public returns (bytes32) {
    bytes32 id = testScheduleProposalSafeSucceeds();

    vm.prank(address(safe));
    timelock.cancel(id); // <@audit Test doesn't verify cancelled ops can't be executed

    assertFalse(
        timelock.isOperation(id), "operation should no longer be present"
    );
    // @audit Missing check that cancelled ops can't pass isOperationReady()
}
```

## Proof of Concept
**Alice (Safe Owner)**
1. Schedules operation X to execute in 2 days
2. Later decides to cancel operation X
3. Calls `cancel(X)`

**Bob (Attacker)**
1. Waits for optimal timing where `block.timestamp < expirationPeriod`
2. Executes cancelled operation X successfully
3. Operation executes despite Safe's cancellation

The root cause is because the `cancel()` function uses `delete` which sets `timestamps[id]` to 0 rather than properly invalidating it. This interacts badly with `isOperationReady()` checks in the execution path.

```
1. Initial setup:
- Safe schedules operation with id X
- timestamp[X] = block.timestamp + delay
- _liveProposals contains X

2. Cancellation:
- Safe calls cancel(X)
- _liveProposals removes X
- timestamp[X] = 0 (due to delete)

3. Execution:
- Attacker waits for block.timestamp < expirationPeriod
- Calls execute() with same parameters
- isOperationReady() passes because:
  - 0 > 1 (false) BUT
  - 0 <= block.timestamp (true) AND
  - 0 + expirationPeriod > block.timestamp (true)
- Operation executes despite cancellation
```
The vulnerability connects

* `cancel()` → `timestamps` storage → `isOperationReady()` → `execute()`
* Missing test coverage in `testCancelActiveProposalSafeSucceeds()`

This creates a complete path for the vulnerability to manifest.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
```diff
function cancel(bytes32 id) external onlySafe whenNotPaused {
    require(
        isOperation(id) && _liveProposals.remove(id),
        "Timelock: operation does not exist"
    );
-   delete timestamps[id];
+   timestamps[id] = _DONE_TIMESTAMP; // Use sentinel value that fails isOperationReady
    emit Cancelled(id);
}
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/InstanceDeployer.sol#L386


# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept

For context, there is a Delegatecall injection in the following function that leads to RCE: 

```solidity
require(
            Safe(payable(walletInstance.safe)).execTransaction(
                multicall3,
                0,
                abi.encodeWithSelector(IMulticall3.aggregate3.selector, calls3),
                Enum.Operation.DelegateCall,
                0,
                0,
                0,
                address(0),
                payable(0),
                signature
            ),
            "InstanceDeployer: Safe delegate call failed"
        );


The key here is that delegatecall allows code execution within the context of the Gnosis Safe wallet (walletInstance.safe). The attacker’s goal is to gain control over the data passed in calls3 and inject malicious delegate calls. Of note is that the calls3 array holds a series of calls that are passed to the Multicall3 contract. Since there is no authentication or access control enforcing who can propose or manage the calls3 array, an external and unauthorized attacker could inject arbitrary delegatecall transactions.

No Access Control on execTransaction: The execTransaction function of the Safe contract is exposed without additional access checks. This lack of authentication or authorization control at the point where calls3 is passed allows any external actor to potentially create malicious inputs for the calls3 array. The input is NOT validated or restricted, meaning that an attacker can insert malicious data targeting the Safe's critical functions, such as changing ownership or transferring funds.

This code involves a delegatecall via the Gnosis Safe's execTransaction function.

By using IMulticall3.aggregate3.selector and passing the calls3 array, the contract allows arbitrary transactions to be executed. Since delegatecall executes the code within the context of the calling contract (in this case, the Safe contract), an attacker can manipulate the calls3 array to execute (arbitrary) malicious code.


After reviewing the path that leads to this function call, I confirmed first that there is no specific access control or authentication mechanisms appear to restrict who can supply the calls3 data. In particular I examined:

--InstanceDeployer.sol does not impose checks on the origin of the calls3 array or the parameters within.
--The Safe contract's execTransactionFromModule function directly processes the delegatecall without validating the calls3 array.
--There is NO validation to ensure that only trusted addresses are used in the calls3 array, making this exploitable if an attacker can inject malicious data.


Ok, similar to the other delegatecall injection I have reported, first step to exploit this vuln is to create a malicious contract that includes a function to change the ownership of the Safe contract.

```solidity
contract MaliciousContract {
    function changeOwnership(address newOwner) public {
        GnosisSafe(targetSafe).transferOwnership(newOwner);
    }
}
```

Then, construct a calls3 array with a single malicious entry pointing to this contract:

```solidity 
IMulticall3.Call3;
calls3[0].target = address(maliciousContract);
calls3[0].callData = abi.encodeWithSelector(MaliciousContract.changeOwnership.selector, newOwner);
calls3[0].allowFailure = false;
```

Then, execute the transaction: 

```solidity 
Safe(walletInstance.safe).execTransactionFromModule(
    multicall3,
    0,
    abi.encodeWithSelector(IMulticall3.aggregate3.selector, calls3),
    Enum.Operation.DelegateCall
);
```
Since delegatecall executes in the context of the Safe, an attacker can gain complete control over Safe operations, including ownership changes and fund transfers, by crafting malicious calls3 entries.

Also, there is no verification or access control on who can manipulate the calls3 array and trigger execTransaction. This makes the Safe contract vulnerable to external manipulation.



Explain and rationalize the potential impact. Provide:
- Direct links to all referenced code in GitHub

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/InstanceDeployer.sol#L386

Impacts from this vulnerability being exploited: 

-->> Ownership/takeover of the Gnosis Safe Wallet

     By crafting a malicious calls3 entry, an attacker can execute any code within the context of the 
     Gnosis Safe wallet. Specifically, as shown in the Proof of Concept (PoC), a malicious contract 
     can transfer ownership of the Safe contract, essentially giving full control to the 
     attacker.

     The Safe contract is responsible for managing assets. By transferring ownership to a malicious 
     actor, they can effectively control all assets within the wallet. This means they could:
     -Modify Safe's parameters
     -Disable security features
     -Prevent legitimate owners from accessing their assets

-->> Unrestricted funds transfer
      An attacker can not only take ownership, but also directly transfer funds by manipulating the 
      calls3 array to include instructions to send funds from the wallet to an arbitrary address

      Since delegatecall executes in the context of the Safe contract, any function that can be executed 
      within the Safe can be hijacked. This includes functions for transferring Ether or tokens stored 
      within the wallet.

-->> Execution of Arbitrary Code 
      The delegatecall mechanism allows arbitrary code execution within the Safe's context. An attacker 
      could inject a wide range of functions, not just changing ownership or transferring funds. For 
      example, they could:
       - Disable or modify critical security mechanisms.
       - Alter the Safe's configuration, making it more vulnerable to future attacks.
       - Deploy persistent backdoors into the wallet.

     Since the calls3 array is not authenticated or validated, any function within the Safe’s scope can 
     be called, making this vulnerability extremely dangerous.

 -->> Lack of Access Controls expands the attack surface 

     The absence of access control means any external actor can craft malicious inputs for the calls3 
     array. This broadens the range of attackers, from internal actors to external adversaries who have 
     no prior access or knowledge of the system.

     Without any form of input validation or role-based access control, the vulnerability becomes 
     accessible to anyone, increasing the chances of exploitation.


  -->> there is also the chance of DoS.

         An attacker could inject calls that modify the Safe in such a way that legitimate users are 
         locked out. This could be through modifying the ownership structure, locking the wallet in an 
         unusable state, or exhausting gas in a way that blocks future transactions.

         By modifying the logic of the Safe using delegatecall, an attacker could effectively "brick" 
         the wallet, rendering it non-functional.




- Screenshots, logs, or any other relevant proof that illustrates the concept
- Any additional research or code needed to validate the claims made in your submission

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Some recommended mitigations are as follows. 

-->>Input validation.  Introduce validation to ensure only trusted addresses, and calls can be made via calls3. Validate function selectors and target addresses.

-->>Role-Based Access Control.  Implement access control for who can execute transactions involving the Safe’s delegatecall functionality. This prevents unauthorized parties from initiating potentially dangerous calls.

-->>Limit the use of Delegatecall.  Reduce the use of delegatecall wherever possible, and avoid using it with user-provided data like calls3.

# Vulnerability details

## Summary

Currently using the `updatePauseDuration()` the timelock is able to immediately cancel the pause no matter what duration is set.

## Vulnerability details

#### Original functionality

Once pause started it could not be disabled anyway. Best case scenario Timelock could call updatePauseDuration and reduce the duration **one day**.

To fix the bug of extending pause duration using `updatePauseDuration(uint128 newPauseDuration)` and bringing back the contracts into the state of paused. But this introduces an unintended side-effect:

It is now possible (intentionally or otherwise) to immediately ended pause whenever the update is called. Because it sets the pauseStartTime to 0.

## Proof of Concept

Sequence of actions:
- PauseGuardian calls pause() -> pauseStartTime = now; paused() returns true
- Timelock calls updatePauseDuration() -> pauseStartTime = 0; paused() returns true (no matter what newPeriod is passed)
- Contract is no longer paused.

Manual Review

Even though the comments in _updatePauseDuration, say

There is nothing preventing it from calling it.

# Vulnerability details

**Description**

The `execute` function is susceptible to front-running. In this function, users can submit transaction details such as target, value, payload, and salt in cleartext calldata. Since these parameters are visible on the blockchain before transaction execution, a malicious actor could monitor pending transactions in the mempool, intercepting and replicating them with potentially modified parameters (such as redirecting target to an address they control or modifying value).

This vulnerability can be particularly problematic in high-stakes environments, where the function interacts with valuable assets or executes critical contract logic. Attackers could manipulate transaction ordering by paying higher gas fees, ensuring their malicious transaction is executed before the original.

**Scenario:**

User submits a transaction using the execute function with a specific target, value, payload, and salt.

Parameters for this transaction become visible in the mempool while awaiting execution.

**Attack Execution:**

An attacker monitors the mempool for execute transactions and notices the pending transaction.

The attacker crafts a similar transaction, possibly modifying parameters like target or value, but keeping the core elements to ensure it passes basic checks.

By setting a higher gas fee, the attacker’s transaction is mined before the original, effectively front-running the user.

**Impact:**

Depending on the modifications, the attacker may redirect funds or alter execution results to their advantage, compromising the function's integrity.

**Recommendation**

To mitigate this front-running vulnerability, consider implementing one or more of the following strategies:

- Commit-Reveal Scheme: Use a commit-reveal mechanism to conceal transaction details until execution. In this method, users first submit a commitment hash of the transaction details. Only after this commitment phase does the actual transaction get revealed and executed. This approach hides transaction parameters from potential attackers, effectively preventing front-running.

- Dynamic Salt or Randomization: Introduce a dynamic salt mechanism that depends on unpredictable factors, such as block details, timestamp, or random oracle inputs, if available. This reduces the predictability of transaction details, increasing the difficulty for front-runners to replicate transactions accurately.

- Shorter Execution Window: Limit the time window during which transactions are valid and monitor pending transactions for unusually long periods. Shorter time windows reduce the chances for attackers to observe and replicate transaction details.

- Gas Price Control and Ordering: To reduce the risk of front-running based on gas prices, encourage users to submit transactions with appropriately competitive gas fees. Alternatively, consider implementing mechanisms to adjust gas prices dynamically or execute transactions based on factors other than gas fees.

By applying these strategies, you can significantly reduce the risk of front-running attacks on the execute function, ensuring a more secure contract execution process.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L687-L700


# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept

The Timelock contract has a `pause` function that pauses and deletes all `activeProposals` that were scheduled before or have already expired but were not cleaned up (https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/ab89bcb443249e1524496b694ddb19e298dca799/src/Timelock.sol#L691-L692). Because we simply iterate over all `liveProposals` without any restrictions (an unbounded array), this means that more proposals result in a more expensive `pause` function, and in some circumstances, this could become an issue. For example:

1. One of the HotSigner's private keys is compromised, and a malicious user can now schedule their transactions.
2. The attacker schedules many transactions, making the `liveProposals` array very large.
3. The `PauseGuardian` tries to call `pause` to stop the spam, allowing time to address the leaked private key.
4. Since `liveProposals` already contains over 1,000 entities, the loop that deletes each entity exceeds the available block gas limit for the current chain, causing the `pause` transaction to fail.

The only available option is to cancel or clean up those proposals manually. However, the problem is that the Timelock allows for the deletion of only one proposal (by id), and there is no batch cancel function. This means deleting entities one by one is ineffective because the attacker can spam transactions at the same or a higher frequency.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Restrict the number of proposals a user can schedule, and add a function to cancel or clean up several proposal IDs at once.


## Assessed type

DoS

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/main/src/Timelock.sol#L378-L387


# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/main/src/Timelock.sol#L378-L387
```sol
    /// @notice supports 1155 and 721 receiver
    /// also supports ERC165 interface id
    function supportsInterface(bytes4 interfaceId)
        public
        view
        override(IERC165, AccessControlEnumerable)
        returns (bool)
    {
        return interfaceId == type(IERC1155Receiver).interfaceId
            || interfaceId == type(IERC721Receiver).interfaceId
            || super.supportsInterface(interfaceId);
    }
```
The contract supports ERC1155 and ERC721 interfaces, but we found that the supportsInterface function did not return true for ERC1155 and ERC721 interfaces when called, which means that ERC1155 and ERC721 interfaces are not supported.
In addition to supporting 1155 and 721 receivers, their own interfaces must also be supported.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
```
function supportsInterface(bytes4 interfaceId)
    public
